title: What If America Was Called 'Alleghania'?
summary:
Have you ever wondered why our country is called the United States of America? It wasn't always that name! When the founders were creating a new country, they had to pick a name. Some ideas were the United Colonies, the United Colonies of America, and even the United States of Alleghania (that's a mouthful!).

Back in 1776, the thirteen colonies were fighting for independence from Great Britain. They knew they had to stick together to win. Thomas Paine, who wrote a famous pamphlet called Common Sense, said they should be the "United Colonies." Benjamin Franklin even drew a picture of a snake cut into pieces with the words "Join, or Die" to show that they needed to unite!

On September 9, 1776, the Continental Congress decided to change the name from "United Colonies" to "United States." But here's a cool detail: in the Declaration of Independence, the word "united" is written with a lowercase "u"! That wasn't a mistake. The founders wanted to emphasize that each state was its own thing. They didn't think of themselves as one nation yet. People said things like "I am a Virginian" first.

Later, in 1781, the Articles of Confederation officially used the name "The United States of America." But the government was weak—it couldn't even collect taxes! So in 1789, they wrote a new Constitution, which is still used today. In the Constitution, the "U" in "United" is capitalized, showing that the country was becoming more united.

So next time you say "United States," remember it could have been "Alleghania"—and that the little letter "u" has a big story!
why_it_matters: The next time you say United States, the name is a clue: it came from thirteen different colonies learning to act like a team, just as people with different backgrounds can come together today.

background_read: In 1776, the eastern part of North America contained thirteen colonies ruled by Great Britain.
Thomas Paine, a writer who wanted America to be free, used his pamphlet Common Sense to encourage independence.
The Continental Congress was the group of colony leaders that made important decisions such as choosing the official name of the new country.
Article_Structure: WHO: The founders, including Thomas Paine and Benjamin Franklin, and the Continental Congress made the name decision.
WHAT: The story of how the country's name changed from United Colonies to United States and then to The United States of America.
WHERE: In the new nation formed from the thirteen colonies that had just declared independence from Great Britain.
WHY: The different names and even the lowercase u show how Americans slowly started to see themselves as one country instead of separate states.

perspectives.description: They wanted United in the name because the colonies had to work together to win independence and build a lasting country.

perspectives.perspective: Leaders who worried about too much power
perspectives.description: They liked keeping states separate and powerful, which is why united was written with a lowercase u and people said things like I am a Virginian first.
They see the lowercase u and the weak government under the Articles of Confederation as signs that the United States became more united over time.
